Healthcare providers should also ensure their patients have up-to-date contact information and a plan for quickly accessing medical care if needed during a crisis. Finally, public education plays a vital role in preparing individuals for power outages. A community should work to raise awareness about the unique needs of individuals who rely on powered medical devices. Community outreach efforts, such as workshops, information campaigns, and training programs, can help individuals understand the importance of having backup power systems and emergency plans in place. The US Department of Health and Human Services has created a workbook for users of home medical devices to assist in establishing a home energy plan. A potential community project could be the distribution of this workbook or a similar planning document to community members, in partnership with healthcare institutions and emergency government. This type of project could also help families, friends, 35 and neighbors of those with medical needs become more aware of how to assist in the event of an emergency, creating a more supportive and resilient community overall. By taking these essential actions—providing access to backup power, ensuring communication, collaborating with healthcare professionals, and increasing public awareness—emergency managers can significantly reduce the risks associated with power outages for individuals who rely on powered medical devices. The success of these strategies depends on thorough planning, collaboration, and ongoing support to ensure the safety and well-being of vulnerable populations during power disruptions. Temperature-Sensitive Medicine Minimum Resilience Standard: All community members dependent upon temperature- sensitive medicine should have an essential medicine emergency plan for maintaining the temperature of the medicine and establishing safe use or replacement protocols for any medicine that may be compromised during a power outage. Vulnerability: Certain populations are more likely to be prescribed temperature-sensitive medicines due to their specific health conditions or treatment needs. These medicines often require careful storage to maintain their effectiveness and safety. The populations most likely to be prescribed temperature-sensitive medicines include people with diabetes, autoimmune disorders, chronic inflammatory conditions, cancer, severe allergies, asthma, hormonal disorders, hemophilia or other bleeding disorders, immune deficiency, or undergoing a transplant, fertility treatment, or taking certain antiviral, antifungal, or antibiotics. Potential Distributed Actions: Individuals with temperature-sensitive medications should have a backup cooling plan if they lose power. Plans should include the temperature medications need to stay and detail what happens to a medication if it becomes too warm or cool. Individuals can use coolers and ice packs or other frozen objects to control the temperature of medications when it is no longer safe to keep them in the refrigerator. Potential Shared Solutions: If an individual with temperature-sensitive medications is unable to safely store medications in their home, they should have priority access to refrigeration at Resilience Hubs or other powered facilities when power is out to ensure the health and safety of that individual.
